title: Propaganda and Public Opinion: Lippmann and Lasswell

ctx-acids.prompt: How does Lasswell use the newspaper’s image (“the public mind is a pool, the propagandist drops acids into it”) in his book?
options: As a summary of his own theory, to argue that the propagandist steers the masses with total control.
He reports it as an image of “all-knowing” foresight imputed to the propagandist; he says that to approach it, methods of testing beforehand would have to be developed.
As proof that propaganda is useless.
As a reply to Lippmann’s book.
ctx-acids.explain: Lasswell brings the quotation in to show the all-knowing quality once imputed to the propagandist, and writes that the propagandist will come somewhat closer to it only if methods of prior testing can be found. The first option is tempting because the image looks very much like the textbook “hypodermic” story; but the quotation is a reported newspaper image, not a summary of theory. The third option goes to the other extreme: Lasswell counts propaganda among the three chief instruments, he does not call it useless. The fourth option does not fit the dates either: the quotation comes from a 1918 newspaper, years before Lippmann’s book.

ctx-war.prompt: Which of the following is a connection supported by the sources we rely on in this lesson?
options: Lippmann was deputy chairman of the Committee on Public Information.
In his 1927 book Lasswell mentions the newcomers to the propaganda or publicity profession and lists Bernays’s 1923 book in his bibliography.
Lasswell was chairman of the Committee on Public Information.
Lasswell and Lippmann ran the same propaganda unit during the war.
ctx-war.explain: The opening pages of Lasswell’s book speak of the new propaganda/publicity profession and of the books by Bernays and by Wilder and Buell; his note on bibliography also lists Bernays’s Crystallizing Public Opinion (1923). The other options sound plausible, but there is no source to rest them on: the committee’s chairman was George Creel; Lippmann served in military intelligence and we found no source for a post of his in the committee; Lasswell was still young during the war (born 1902), and there is no source for a joint unit either.

who-when.prompt: Dewey’s The Public and Its Problems was published before Lippmann’s The Phantom Public.
who-when.explain: The Phantom Public came out in 1925, Dewey’s book in 1927. The trap: Dewey’s New Republic reviews (1922, 1925) and his lectures (1926) really are earlier; but the question asks about the book, and its printed form appeared in 1927, after both of Lippmann’s books. “Reply” means “later” in order.

claim-lippmann.prompt: In a neighbourhood everyone carries their own picture of the rumour that “parking will become paid”. Hundreds of people, acting on the same picture, file a joint petition with the municipality. In Lippmann’s distinction, what do we call the pictures that turned into the petition?
options: Public opinions in small letters, because everyone’s picture is different.
Public Opinion in capital letters, because they are pictures turned into action in the name of a group.
Not a pseudo-environment but the real environment, because people acted.
Not public opinion at all, because no poll was taken.
claim-lippmann.explain: For Lippmann the pictures in people’s heads are their public opinions, and those acted upon by groups are Public Opinion with capital letters. The first option correctly sees that pictures differ from person to person but skips the test of turning into action. The third option confuses action with the reality of the environment: a picture that moves people is still a picture, and its consequences show up in the real environment. The fourth option uses a poll as the criterion; Lippmann’s definition has no such criterion.

claim-lasswell.prompt: A commander visits the front, increases the soldiers’ cigarette and food rations, and morale rises. According to Lasswell’s definition, what is this?
options: Propaganda, because it raised morale.
Not propaganda: it changes an objective condition, whereas propaganda manages opinion through significant symbols.
Only the cigarette ration is propaganda.
Military pressure.
claim-lasswell.explain: Lasswell leaves out exactly this example: raising morale by changing objective conditions such as the cigarette supply or the composition of food is not propaganda; propaganda manages opinion through symbols, stories, reports and pictures. The first option rests on the intuition “if it influences, it is propaganda”; Lasswell takes the kind of means, not the fact of influence, as his criterion. In the fourth option, military pressure means the coercive power of land, sea and air forces; a treat does not belong in that class.

concepts-glossary.prompt: Match each concept with its definition.
pairs: The representation between a person and the real environment, to which behaviour responds
The pattern supplied by culture that lets us define first and see afterwards
Pictures acted upon by groups or in the name of groups
Independent expert bureaus showing decision-makers the facts they cannot see
concepts-glossary.explain: A pseudo-environment is a representation, not a lie; a stereotype is the ready-made piece that fills that representation. Capital-letter Public Opinion is the acted-upon form of pictures. Organized intelligence is Lippmann’s remedy: experts do not rule, they show decision-makers the facts. The pair most often confused is pseudo-environment and stereotype: one is the frame, the other the pattern that fills it.

assump-lippmann.prompt: A doctor can form views on matters outside medicine, for example international trade agreements, only from the news. According to Lippmann’s sentence “every one of us is an outsider”, what is the doctor’s situation?
options: A lack of intelligence: the doctor is uneducated on these matters.
A matter of position: on this subject the doctor too is an outsider, with limited time, attention and specialist equipment.
It applies only to people who do not read newspapers.
It proves that experts should govern the people.
assump-lippmann.explain: For Lippmann, being an outsider is not a personal defect but a limit tied to position: everyone is an outsider in most fields, doctors included. The first option is exactly the “the people are stupid” reading and does not fit the text. The third option ties the limit to newspaper reading, while it comes from time, attention and equipment. The fourth option drags Lippmann towards elitism, but the experts he proposes do not govern; they supply facts to decision-makers.

assump-phantom.prompt: A voter says she will not vote for the governing party, influenced only by corruption stories, without knowing the technical details of a municipal tender. How does the notion of the public in The Phantom Public read this behaviour?
options: As an example of the public scrutinising the tender in detail.
As the public taking sides for or against the actors, that is, intervening from outside.
As an example of the public writing policy.
As proof that the public has disappeared.
assump-phantom.explain: Lippmann’s public judges the actors on stage, not the details: it takes sides for or against an actor and intervenes from outside. The first and third options load onto the public jobs Lippmann leaves out of its remit (detailed scrutiny, writing policy). The fourth option takes the word “phantom” literally: Lippmann does not say the public does nothing, he says there is no fixed public steering events.

how-lippmann.prompt: Put the links of Lippmann’s account in order.
items: Access to a distant event is limited
The short messages that arrive are completed by stereotypes in the head
The completed picture fuses with the person’s own interests
The person or group acts on the picture
The consequences appear in the real environment and the mismatch is felt
how-lippmann.explain: The order: first the limits of access, then completion by stereotypes, then fusion with interests, then acting on the picture, and finally the collision in the real environment. The most common mistake is to put the consequences first: for Lippmann behaviour is steered from the pseudo-environment, but the consequences are paid in the real environment; that is why the error is usually visible last.

how-propaganda.prompt: A propaganda bureau hands the same factory workers two leaflets: one in the morning saying “the war is the rich men’s business”, one in the evening saying “the war is the common cause of all classes”. Which principle in Lasswell’s book is broken?
options: The principle of choosing one of the four strategic aims.
The principle of not giving contradictory messages, in the same context, to the same or closely connected groups.
The principle of using the streetcar as a carrier.
The principle of working on the enemy’s morale.
how-propaganda.explain: Lasswell writes that propaganda must avoid self-contradiction in the same context when addressed to the same group or to groups in close contact; the Protestant and Catholic example rests on exactly this. Since the leaflets go to the same workers, the second option is correct. The first option catches the eye, but the problem is not that no aim was chosen; it is that two opposed messages reach the same audience. The third and fourth options are details unrelated to the example.

ev-goettingen.prompt: Which is the most reasonable assessment of how strong the Göttingen account is as evidence?
options: The observers deliberately lied; the account shows people’s dishonesty.
Lippmann argues that the observers saw their own stereotypes; but the account is a single staged event reported at second hand: it brings the concept to life without proving it generalises.
The experiment proves that trained observers can never be reliable.
Because the scene was staged in advance, the experiment is worthless.
ev-goettingen.explain: Lippmann bases his reading on the concept of the stereotype; but what we have is one event reported from a French source, so it is an example, not a measurement. The first option assumes intent; Lippmann says the opposite: the observers were not lying, they saw what did not happen. The third option draws an absolute conclusion from one event. The fourth is wrong too: staging the event is how the reports can be compared with a known reality; it does not make the experiment worthless.

ev-records.prompt: In his 1927 book Lasswell measured the effect of propaganda with surveys of audiences.
ev-records.explain: The book’s note on bibliography shows that the material was printed documents, memoirs and hearings; and in the text he writes that the result would improve if methods of prior testing could be devised. So the book is an analysis of documents, not a measurement of audiences. The trap is to assume that every classic book about “propaganda” contains audience experiments.

crit-debate.prompt: According to Schudson’s 2008 article, which is the most accurate statement about the “Lippmann–Dewey debate”?
options: In the 1920s the two authors conducted an open debate by publishing replies to each other.
The “debate” consisted of Dewey’s reviews and his 1927 book; Lippmann did not reply, and the “debate” frame was constructed in the 1980s–90s.
Dewey only criticised Lippmann’s books.
The debate rests on letters discovered in the 1980s.
crit-debate.explain: Schudson’s finding: the “debate” consists of Dewey’s favourable reviews plus the 1927 book, Lippmann did not respond, and the frame is a product of the 1980s–90s. The first option is exactly that frame. The third option leaves out that Dewey’s reviews were favourable. The fourth is invented: what we have is not a story based on letters but a narrative constructed later.

crit-dewey.prompt: One city sets up an expert bureau that presents water-quality measurements only to the council members who will decide (A). Another city publishes the same measurements in plain reports and holds open meetings where citizens can discuss them (B). Which arrangement is closer to Dewey’s emphasis?
options: A, because experts should decide.
B, because the essential need is to improve the conditions of debate and persuasion, and citizens must be able to judge the bearing of the findings.
Both, because Dewey gives experts no role at all.
Neither, because Dewey argues that the public is a phantom.
crit-dewey.explain: Dewey expects facts from experts and wants the public to be able to judge how those facts bear on its own concerns; the way to that is better conditions of discussion and persuasion. A is closer to Lippmann’s intelligence bureau: the facts go to decision-makers. The third option assumes Dewey gives experts no role, but he accepts them as finders of facts. The fourth attributes the word “phantom” to Dewey; that word is Lippmann’s, and Dewey’s answer is “eclipse”.

crit-frame.prompt: The mechanism in Lippmann’s account is that the message acts directly and unobstructed on the receiver.
crit-frame.explain: In Lippmann’s account the message passes through limits of access and stereotypes, fuses with the person’s interests and has its consequences tested in the real environment. “Direct and unobstructed” operation is the hypodermic caricature drawn by textbooks; it is not the logic of Lippmann’s own book.

today-feeds.prompt: A study finds that more than 85 per cent of the topics on Twitter’s “trending” list are news-related. What is the most cautious reading in Lippmann’s framework?
options: It shows that Twitter has abolished news.

Much of the agenda on the screen may be the circulation of a picture drawn by news production; it may be multiplying the old pseudo-environment rather than creating a new one (our inference, not proven).
It shows that users do not believe the news.
It shows that stereotypes have ended.
today-feeds.explain: The finding says that most trending topics come from news; the inference “the screen is an echo of the news picture” is reasonable but it is our interpretation, not the study’s result. The first option turns the finding upside down: the topics turned out to be news-based. The third option speaks about belief, and the finding is not about belief. The fourth says stereotypes ended; the finding says nothing about stereotypes.

today-lab-news.prompt: In the lab a friend writes “the papers made up the panic”. Given Lippmann’s warning that “fictions are not lies”, which is the most accurate correction?
options: Leave it as it is; newspapers always lie.
The picture the papers drew may misrepresent reality; that need not mean deliberate invention, and intent needs separate evidence.
Write that there was no panic at all.
Add that stereotypes occur only in newspapers.
today-lab-news.explain: A pseudo-environment is a representation; it can be incomplete, slanted or late, and showing that it was made on purpose is a separate claim. The first option assumes intent. The third is excessive: some listeners were frightened. The fourth locks stereotypes into newspapers; for Lippmann a stereotype is in everybody’s head.

today-lab-consent.prompt: In the 1922 paragraph Lippmann also writes that nobody yet grasps the consequences of “creating consent”.
today-lab-consent.explain: The paragraph contains the sentence “None of us begins to understand the consequences”: Lippmann says a revolution is taking place but adds that its consequences are not understood. The thought that would lead you to the wrong answer is that the paragraph is praise or a recommendation; the text itself does neither openly.

exam-patterns.prompt: In an exam the question “Which of the following does NOT belong to Lippmann?” has these options: pseudo-environment; stereotype; the manufacture of consent; the engineering of consent. Which is the correct option?
options: Pseudo-environment
Stereotype
The manufacture of consent
The engineering of consent
exam-patterns.explain: “Engineering of consent” is the title of Bernays’s 1947 article. The other three are in Lippmann’s 1922 book. The most common mistake is to mix up the verbs “manufacture” and “engineering”: the first is Lippmann’s, the second Bernays’s.

summary.prompt: In both books of this lesson the audience is described as a passive target that takes in the message like an injection.
summary.explain: In both books the audience is equipped with stereotypes, interests and existing group inclinations: in Lippmann the message passes through stereotypes and limits of access and is tested in the real environment; in Lasswell the propagandist usually facilitates a group’s existing inclinations. The “passive target” story is the textbooks’ caricature.

quiz.prompt: Match each concept or phrase with its source.
pairs: Pseudo-environment and the pictures in our heads
Propaganda: managing opinion through significant symbols
quiz.explain: The picture and the pseudo-environment belong to Lippmann’s 1922 book; the phantom public to his 1925 book; the definition of propaganda to Lasswell’s 1927 book; the image of eclipse to Dewey’s 1927 book; “engineering of consent” to Bernays’s 1947 article. The pairs most often confused: phantom (Lippmann) and eclipse (Dewey), and manufacture (Lippmann) and engineering (Bernays).

quiz.prompt: Put these publications in order of publication, oldest first.
items: Lasswell: Propaganda Technique in the World War
quiz.explain: The order: Public Opinion (1922), The Phantom Public (1925), Propaganda Technique in the World War (1927), “The Engineering of Consent” (1947), Manufacturing Consent (1988). Memory hook: picture, phantom, technique; then two “consent” names: Bernays 25 years after Lippmann, Herman and Chomsky 66 years after.

quiz.text: According to Lippmann, a person responds not to the real environment but to the {{1}} in his head; this representation is called the {{2}} environment. According to Lasswell, propaganda is the management of opinions and attitudes through {{3}}.

options: picture
law
measurement
pseudo
natural
economic
the direct manipulation of significant symbols
changing objective conditions
military pressure

quiz.explain: In Lippmann behaviour responds to the picture in the head (the pseudo-environment), not to the environment itself. In Lasswell’s definition propaganda manages opinion through symbols; changing objective conditions or military pressure are other instruments. The trap is to choose “changing objective conditions” in the third blank: Lasswell leaves that outside propaganda.

quiz.prompt: The phrase “manufacture of consent” was first used in Herman and Chomsky’s 1988 book.
quiz.explain: The phrase occurs in Lippmann’s 1922 Public Opinion; Herman and Chomsky made it the title of their book, and Chomsky said Lippmann invented the phrase. The trap is to think the book title gave birth to the phrase. (Bernays’s 1947 phrase is different: “engineering of consent”.)

quiz.scenario: A district newspaper reports on a distant dam project for three days under the headline “destructive flood risk”; its only source is a short statement from the municipality. Readers quickly sign petitions. A week later a report by an independent body shows that the risk is low. (Hypothetical scenario.)

parts.prompt: In Lippmann’s terms, what is the picture the petitioners acted on?
options: A pseudo-environment
The real environment
A phantom public
parts.explain: The readers responded to the picture the report drew, that is, to a pseudo-environment; the result (the petition) appeared in the real environment, and the report then showed the real environment. The “real environment” option confuses the picture with the event itself; “phantom public” is a concept about the public, not the picture.

parts.prompt: Which step is closest to Lippmann’s 1922 remedy?
options: Banning the newspaper
Setting up an independent intelligence/expert bureau that shows decision-makers the facts
Expecting every citizen to learn dam engineering
parts.explain: Lippmann’s proposal is independent expert bureaus that show decision-makers the facts they cannot see; the aim is not to load expert work onto every citizen. The third option is the “omnicompetent citizen” assumption, the very thing Lippmann criticises. The first option is a measure that has no place in Lippmann.

parts.prompt: How does Dewey’s emphasis apply to this scenario?
options: Only the experts in the bureau should decide
The findings should circulate in a form citizens can discuss and judge, and communication needs to be improved
There is no public, so the petition is meaningless
parts.explain: Dewey sees the expert as a finder of facts and says the essential need is to improve the conditions of debate, discussion and persuasion; citizens must be able to judge how the knowledge bears on their concerns. The first option is closer to Lippmann’s reading; the third attributes Lippmann’s “phantom” claim to Dewey.

quiz.takeaway: A pseudo-environment needs no bad faith; an incomplete picture is enough. Lippmann looks for the remedy in showing decision-makers the facts they cannot see; Dewey looks for it in improving the conditions under which those facts reach the public.

quiz.prompt: Which of the following is NOT one of the wartime propaganda aims listed in Lasswell’s 1927 book?
options: To mobilise hatred against the enemy
To preserve the friendship of allies
To preserve the friendship and, if possible, procure the co-operation of neutrals
To silence domestic political opposition by law
quiz.explain: Lasswell lists four aims: to mobilise hatred against the enemy, to preserve the friendship of allies, to preserve the friendship and if possible procure the co-operation of neutrals, and to demoralise the enemy. Silencing opposition by law is a form of legal coercion and falls outside Lasswell’s definition of managing opinion through symbols. In “NOT” questions the most common mistake is to tick a sentence that merely looks right.

quiz.prompt: Which is one reason, according to Lippmann, why stereotypes are so resistant?
options: Simply laziness: people do not want to think.
They are a defence of the person’s position in society and self-respect; whatever shakes them feels like an attack on “the foundations of the universe”.
Newspapers reproduce them every day.
They are protected by law.
quiz.explain: In chapter VII, besides economy of effort, Lippmann adds a second reason: stereotypes defend the person’s position, self-respect and tradition; that is why shaking them feels like an attack on “our universe”. The first option sees only economy of effort and misses the second reason. The third and fourth options are not reasons argued in that chapter.

quiz.prompt: According to Lippmann, the public is a fixed body of citizens that steers the course of events.
quiz.explain: In The Phantom Public Lippmann writes the opposite: such a public is “a mere phantom”, an abstraction; the public is a changing set of people who are interested in an affair and can affect it only by supporting or opposing the actors. The trap is to read “phantom” as “the public does nothing”.

quiz.prompt: Which is true of Dewey’s stance in his 1927 book?
options: He gave experts no role at all.
He said the public is in eclipse and the remedy lies in improving communication and the conditions of debate and persuasion; he defined the experts’ job as discovering and making known the facts.
He wrote before Lippmann that the public is a phantom.
He never cited Lippmann’s books.
quiz.explain: Dewey sees the expert not as the maker of policy but as the person who finds the facts and makes them known, and he looks for the remedy in better communication. The first option erases the experts’ role. The third gives Dewey the “phantom” instead of Lippmann, but that word is Lippmann’s. The fourth is wrong: in a footnote Dewey acknowledges his debt to both of Lippmann’s books.
